Bụ́kụ̃ Núkũtã Ãrị̃ngã Tị sĩjó rĩ ãzíla ífí la icéjó rĩ / Aringa Orthography Spelling and Writing Guide. First edition, revised. Yumbe: Here is Life (HIL) with SIL International Uganda, LABE and MoES Yumbe. ISBN 978-9970-719-24-2. c. 20 pp.
tone_statements.quote: Ãrị̃ngã Tị also has four tones, three of which are marked (low, high, falling) and one which is unmarked (mid). [...] b) Tone. Ãrị̃ngã Tị is a tonal language, therefore pitch can change the meaning of a word (lexical tone) or the part of speech (grammatical tone). It is a language with many monosyllabic or short words where tone has a high functional load. [...] Tones are always connected to vowels so tonal marks shall be written above vowels. The following tones and tone symbols are used in Ãrị̃ngã Tị: i) Low tone, e.g. ã ãmã (our) ii) Mid tone, e.g. a aga (pass exams) iii) High tone, e.g. á ágágá (middle) iv) Falling tone, e.g. â ụrụgâlé (up there)
tone_statements.locator: p. 5 (sec. 3 'Vowels' right half) and pp. 6-7 (sec. 3b 'Tone' left half and p. 13 right half)

Bụ́kụ̃ Anzị ꞌBa Drị́ Núkũtã Ãrị̃ngã Tị Sĩrĩ Sĩŋá Ụ̃nị̃jó Ụ́ꞌdụ́kọ́ Lã Be Rĩ / Learning to read and write Aringa tones and vowels: Student's Book. Revised trial edition. Arua: SIL & Here is Life! Aringa Language Project (Box 26 Yumbe / Box 103 Arua). 27 pp. in the online PDF (SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 54884: 29 pp., subjects Vowel, Tone, Primer, 'Not Available Online'); companion Teacher's Book by the same author = entry 54885, 58 pp.
tone_statements.quote: Any vowel without a tone mark is mid tone. a, e, i, o, u. [...] Falling tone type 1: The first type of falling tone is for words which have falling tone as part of the basic word. The word is always pronounced with a falling tone. [...] Falling tone type 2: The second type of falling tone is due to grammar. Certain words usually do not have falling tone, but can be pronounced as falling tone in certain grammatical phrases. [...] Rising tones are tones that ‘rise’ from a lower tone to a higher tone. Double vowels are usually used. The following combinations are possible: Low-High, Mid-High, and Low-Mid.
tone_statements.locator: p. 6 (Lesson 'Mid Tone'), p. 17 ('Falling Tone', types 1-2; type 3 on p. 18 not), p. 19 ('Rising Tone')
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.n_tones: 3 level (H, M, L) + falling; rising realised as two-vowel sequences (L-H, M-H,…

sources.citation: Kilpatrick, Eileen. 2004. Orthographies of Moru-Ma'di languages. Occasional Papers in the Study of Sudanese Languages 9: 85-91. Entebbe: SIL-Sudan.
sources.note: Nothing. Covers Aringa by name (p. 85) with segment inventory/grapheme charts and a 'Tones' section (p. 88): all Moru-Ma'di languages have three level tones H/M/L; 'Madi and Aringa also use tone to mark singular and plural distinctions'. No occurrence of stress/accent in the prosodic sense.

sources.citation: Boone, Douglas W. & Richard L. Watson (eds.). 1999. Moru-Ma'di survey report. SIL Electronic Survey Reports 1999-001. 260 pp.
sources.note: Nothing (0 prosodic hits for stress/accent in 260 pp). Aringa = northernmost, most divergent Lugbara dialect ('Low Lugbara'); 'On the phonetic level, Aringa and Terego are closer than one would guess from the lexical data'; Appendix 8 notes Tucker's 1940 Lugbara data 'both lexically and phonetically most resembles the Aringa dialect'. Tone marked on wordlists only.

sources.citation: Andersen, Torben. 1986. Tone splitting and vowel quality: evidence from Lugbara. Studies in African Linguistics 17(1): 55-68.
sources.note: Western vs Eastern Lugbara tone; no stress statement; Aringa not treated.

sources.citation: Crothers, J. H. et al. (eds.). 1979. Handbook of Phonological Data from a Sample of the World's Languages (Stanford Phonology Archive), entry 145 Logbara.
sources.note: Second-hand from Tucker & Bryan: stress location varies among Moru-Ma'di languages (Moru initial, Ma'di final); nothing stated for Logbara itself, nothing on Aringa.

sources.note: Tone-literacy primer: lessons on High (á), Mid (unmarked) and Low (ã) tone with key words for HH, MM, LL, MH, HM, LM, LH, ML, HL patterns and minimal-pair sentence drills; Falling tone (â) of three types: (1) lexical, part of the basic word; (2) grammatical, arising in certain grammatical phrases; (3) from two parts of a word coming together, written as two vowels with separate tones; Rising tones written as double vowels (L-H, M-H, L-M); a section 'Tone on Pronouns'. No analytic statement beyond this; nothing on stress.
